resident.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old female presented with a nine-month decline in lower extremity strength and ambulation ability.
resident.history: This 44-year-old female presented with a decline in lower extremity strength and ambulation ability over nine months. She also reported increased numbness of the lower extremities, worsening lower back pain, bowel incontinence, neck pain, and paresthesias, numbness, and weakness of the upper extremities. The record contains no separate laboratory report; any laboratory values reported by the authors are in the case record.
resident.physical_exam: Neurologic examination revealed a motor and sensory deficit in the lower limbs with 3 out of 5 muscle strength and loss of sensation to light touch in the bilateral lower extremities up to the level of the upper thighs. The upper extremities showed 4 out of 5 strength bilaterally, with a notable claw hand deformity of the left hand. Sensation to light touch was diminished in the distal upper extremities. Reflexes were not documented.
key_positive_signs: 3/5 motor strength in bilateral lower extremities
Loss of light touch sensation in bilateral lower extremities up to the upper thighs
Claw hand deformity of the left hand
Diminished light touch sensation in distal upper extremities
Extensive ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) along the spinal cord on CT
Severe central canal stenosis at C3-5, T6-10, and L3-4
Severe bilateral neural foraminal stenosis in cervical and lumbar spine
resident.past_history: Medical history included severe diabetes mellitus complicated by peripheral neuropathy and a foot ulcer, and chronic urinary incontinence treated with a bladder stimulator.
resident.public_message: A 44-year-old female presented with a nine-month history of progressive lower extremity weakness and difficulty walking, along with worsening lower extremity numbness, low back pain, bowel incontinence, neck pain, and upper extremity numbness and weakness. Examination showed 3/5 strength and loss of light touch sensation in bilateral lower extremities up to the upper thighs, 4/5 upper extremity strength, a left claw hand deformity, and diminished distal upper extremity sensation. Reflexes were not documented. CT of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine demonstrated extensive OPLL and severe central canal stenosis at C3-5, T6-10, and L3-4, plus severe bilateral neural foraminal stenosis in the cervical and lumbar spine. Past history includes severe diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy and a foot ulcer, and chronic urinary incontinence treated with a bladder stimulator. No separate laboratory results are documented.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record’s description only; films were not available for review. The record describes extensive OPLL with prominent osteophytes producing severe central canal stenosis at C3-5, T6-10, and L3-4, with severe bilateral neural foraminal stenosis in the cervical and lumbar spine. T6-10 is the dominant reported thoracic region. Compression direction and cord T2 signal are not stated in the record. The multilevel severe stenosis provides moderate correlation with the reported extremity weakness, sensory symptoms, and gait decline, although the record also notes diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

neurology.localization: The clinical picture suggests a compressive myelopathy, most likely from severe central canal stenosis at C3-5 and T6-10, given progressive lower extremity weakness (3/5) and bowel incontinence. Upper extremity weakness (4/5) and distal sensory loss may arise from cervical cord involvement or radiculopathy, but the left claw hand indicates a lower cervical (C8/T1) root or ulnar nerve lesion, not directly from central stenosis at C3-5. The sensory level to light touch at the upper thighs is lower than expected for T6-10 cord compression and likely reflects superimposed diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Reflexes were not documented, so upper motor neuron signs cannot be confirmed; localization rests on an incomplete examination.

red_flags.finding: Long-standing diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy and foot ulcer
red_flags.rationale: This can cause length-dependent sensory loss and contribute to lower extremity weakness, potentially obscuring a cord sensory level; it does not negate the structural cord compression as a cause of progressive weakness and bowel incontinence, so it coexists rather than changes the indication.

red_flags.finding: Left claw hand deformity and distal upper extremity sensory loss
red_flags.rationale: These findings suggest an ulnar neuropathy or C8/T1 radiculopathy, which is not explained by the central stenosis at C3-5 or T6-10. While it may require further evaluation (e.g., EMG/NCS) and could influence cervical foraminal decompression if radicular, it does not alter the primary indication for treating the compressive myelopathy.

red_flags.finding: Chronic urinary incontinence treated with a bladder stimulator
red_flags.rationale: Pre-existing bladder dysfunction limits the specificity of urinary symptoms as a localizing sign for the current cord compression; however, new bowel incontinence remains supportive of myelopathy. This does not change the need to address the stenosis.

Absence of reflex findings prevents confirmation of upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) that would support a myelopathic localization. It does not alter the decision given the severe stenosis but reduces diagnostic certainty.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The sensory level to light touch at the upper thighs corresponds to an L1-2 dermatomal level, which is lower than the expected level from severe T6-10 stenosis; this likely reflects diabetic peripheral neuropathy rather than a true cord level. In addition, the left claw hand is not directly produced by central canal stenosis at C3-5 and suggests a focal ulnar or C8/T1 radicular lesion.
neurology.public_message: Localization: The findings are consistent with multilevel compressive myelopathy, most likely from severe thoracic (T6-10) and/or cervical (C3-5) stenosis, causing progressive lower extremity weakness and bowel dysfunction; however, the examination is incomplete because reflexes were not documented. Coexisting diabetic peripheral neuropathy likely contributes to sensory loss (stocking distribution) and may obscure a cord sensory level. The left claw hand suggests an additional ulnar or C8/T1 radicular process. Red flags: (1) diabetic peripheral neuropathy—coexisting; (2) left claw hand—coexisting (may warrant ulnar nerve/C8-T1 workup but does not change main indication); (3) chronic urinary incontinence with bladder stimulator—coexisting (pre-existing, so urinary symptoms not reliable); (4) absent reflex documentation—coexisting (limits UMN confirmation). Overall match between symptoms and imaging is medium: severe multilevel stenosis explains the dominant syndrome but not every finding.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade: III. Intraoperative MAP target: 70 mmHg. Blood loss risk: high. Extubation difficulty: unassessable due to absence of airway assessment on record. Prone position tolerance: unassessable due to lack of cardiopulmonary assessment.

preconditions_for_failure: Progression of lower extremity weakness (decline of ≥1 MRC grade in any muscle group) despite adherence to therapy
New or worsening bowel or bladder dysfunction (e.g., urinary retention or increasing incontinence episodes)
New or progressive gait deterioration (e.g., loss of ambulation ability or increased falls)
Development of upper motor neuron signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, Babinski, clonus) if previously absent, indicating myelopathy progression
physiatrist_opening.public_message: Severe multilevel OPLL with cord compression and progressive myelopathy is a serious condition, and I acknowledge that many patients with this degree of stenosis and neurologic deficit ultimately require surgical decompression. However, I propose a structured, time-limited conservative trial of 3-6 months involving intensive physical therapy focused on core and postural stabilization, gait training, pain management, and close neurologic monitoring. Some patients with compressive myelopathy can stabilize or improve with such programs, but the success rate in this severe presentation is modest—I estimate around 25% chance of meaningful functional improvement. The patient's diabetic peripheral neuropathy and pre-existing bladder dysfunction complicate clinical assessment, so we must rely on objective serial examinations. I will accept that conservative management has failed if any of the following occur: objective worsening of lower extremity strength, new or progressive bowel/bladder dysfunction, further gait deterioration, or development of upper motor neuron signs. Until such evidence emerges, I advocate for a trial of conservative care before considering surgery.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The director and deputy director have both argued that the progressive lower extremity weakness, sensory level, and bowel incontinence in the setting of severe multilevel OPLL carry an unacceptable risk of irreversible cord injury if we wait 3-6 months. I have already weighed these findings heavily when framing my conservative trial. However, they have not pointed to a specific finding in the record that I have given too little weight. In particular, there is no documented cord T2 signal change, no interval decline between serial neurological examinations, and no upper motor neuron signs. The pre-existing diabetic peripheral neuropathy and chronic urinary incontinence with bladder stimulator confound attribution of the current symptoms solely to acute compressive myelopathy. The claim that 'preconditions for failure would likely be met too late to prevent permanent damage' is a risk assertion, not evidence from this patient's record. A structured, closely monitored 3-6 month trial with predefined failure criteria remains a reasonable option until objective markers of irreversible injury are demonstrated. I hold my stance.

vice_opinions.assessment: This 44-year-old woman has progressive lower extremity weakness (3/5), a sensory level to the upper thighs, and bowel incontinence in the setting of severe multilevel OPLL with central stenosis at C3-5, T6-10, and L3-4. This presentation is most consistent with compressive myelopathy, likely thoracic and/or cervical in origin. Coexisting diabetic neuropathy and chronic bladder dysfunction cloud the clinical picture but do not negate the myelopathy. The progressive course and severity of stenosis carry a high risk of irreversible spinal cord injury if not decompressed promptly. Conservative management is not advisable; a 3-6 month trial would expose the patient to unnecessary risk of permanent neurological decline. Surgical decompression is indicated, but the exact sequence and approach require additional imaging and clinical detail.
proposed_options: Urgent staged surgical decompression of the cervical (C3-5) and thoracic (T6-10) stenosis, with consideration of L3-4 foraminal decompression if radicular symptoms are significant, after obtaining MRI with cord signal, anesthesia clearance, and documenting reflexes.
Conservative management trial for 3-6 months with intensive rehabilitation and strict monitoring for neurological deterioration (physiatrist's proposal).
Focused diagnostic workup (MRI, CT myelogram, reflex exam, urodynamics) and multidisciplinary planning before committing to surgery, while preparing the patient for likely operative intervention.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent staged surgical decompression of the cervical and thoracic stenosis, starting with the level most responsible for the myelopathy (likely thoracic based on lower extremity findings), after rapid preoperative imaging and anesthesia evaluation.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist's recommendation for a 3-6 month conservative trial is not defensible in the setting of progressive myelopathy with severe stenosis and bowel incontinence; delay risks irreversible cord damage.
The primary symptomatic level is uncertain (thoracic vs cervical vs both). We need MRI with T2-weighted cord signal and a complete neurological exam including reflexes to prioritize decompression.

The optimal surgical approach for OPLL (anterior vs posterior, laminectomy/fusion vs laminoplasty) remains unsettled and depends on OPLL morphology and cord compression direction, which are not documented.
Whether to include L3-4 foraminal stenosis in the initial procedure or stage it later is unclear and depends on the contribution of lumbar radiculopathy to the clinical picture.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we proceed directly to urgent surgical planning, or is a short delay (days) for additional imaging and multidisciplinary input acceptable?
If staged surgery is required, which region would you prioritize first: thoracic or cervical?
Do you want a formal spine oncology or thoracic surgery consultation if an anterior thoracic approach is considered for the OPLL?
vice_opinions.public_message: I recommend urgent surgical decompression for this patient. The progressive lower extremity weakness, sensory level, and bowel incontinence with severe multilevel OPLL indicate compressive myelopathy that will not improve with conservative care. While we need MRI and anesthesia clearance, delay should be minimized. I propose staged decompression of the cervical and thoracic stenosis, starting with the level most likely responsible—likely thoracic given the lower extremity findings—but I defer the final decision on sequence and timing to the group.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 44-year-old woman with progressive lower extremity weakness, a sensory level to the upper thighs, and reported bowel incontinence in the setting of severe multilevel OPLL. The clinical picture is most consistent with thoracic myelopathy from T6-10 stenosis, though cervical C3-5 stenosis could contribute and lumbar L3-4 stenosis cannot be fully excluded. The absence of reflex documentation and lack of MRI cord signal data prevent definitive localization. I agree with the director that surgery is indicated and should not be delayed by a 3-6 month conservative trial; however, preoperative MRI and complete neurological examination are necessary to choose the first level.
proposed_options: Perform MRI of the entire spine with emphasis on cord signal change and axial compression at C3-5, T6-10, and L3-4, and complete neurological exam with reflexes; then decompress the thoracic level first if T6-10 is confirmed as dominant.
If MRI shows cervical cord T2 hyperintensity and/or exam suggests cervical myelopathy, decompress C3-5 first and reassess thoracic after recovery.

Consider combined single-stage decompression of thoracic and cervical stenosis only if patient is optimized and imaging shows tandem lesions with both causing significant cord compression; otherwise staged surgery is preferred.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Thoracic decompression first (T6-10), contingent on MRI and reflex findings confirming thoracic dominance over cervical; I would switch to cervical first if cervical cord signal is more severe.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's 3-6 month conservative trial: this patient has progressive myelopathy and delaying decompression risks irreversible cord damage. The proposed failure criteria (new UMN signs, further decline) may be met too late.

The record is inconsistent on bowel function: it lists chronic urinary incontinence with a bladder stimulator but separately reports bowel incontinence. We must clarify whether bowel incontinence is new, as this affects localization and urgency.

Thoracic versus cervical dominance cannot be inferred reliably from the current data because reflexes were not documented and no MRI cord signal is available. I raise this as an open question that imaging must settle.
deferred_questions_to_director: After MRI and exam, if both cervical and thoracic levels show cord T2 hyperintensity, do you favour thoracic-first or cervical-first decompression? I recommend thoracic-first based on lower extremity predominance, but I need your decision.
Should we proceed directly to surgery if MRI shows no T2 signal but clinical progression is ongoing, or would you still require additional imaging?
vice_opinions.public_message: Director, I agree with your decision that surgery is indicated and that we need MRI and a complete neurological exam before final planning. I favour starting with thoracic decompression (T6-10) because the dominant deficits are lower extremity weakness and a sensory level to the upper thighs, and new bowel incontinence localizes more to thoracic cord than cervical. However, I will change my preference to cervical first if the MRI shows cervical cord T2 hyperintensity and the reflex exam reveals upper motor neuron signs with a cervical pattern. We need to resolve the record's discrepancy between chronic urinary incontinence and new bowel incontinence before attributing that symptom. I remain opposed to a 3-6 month conservative trial as delay risks irreversible cord injury. Please confirm after MRI whether you accept thoracic-first staging or if you would prioritize cervical based on findings.

director_rulings.public_message: I have heard all perspectives. The progressive lower extremity weakness, sensory level, and bowel incontinence with severe multilevel OPLL strongly indicate compressive myelopathy, and the physiatrist's proposed 3-6 month conservative trial is not acceptable given the risk of irreversible cord injury; the preconditions for failure would likely be met too late to prevent permanent damage. director_rulings.final_decision: Surgery is indicated for progressive myelopathy from multilevel OPLL. We will not accept a 3-6 month conservative trial because delay risks irreversible cord injury. We need urgent MRI and complete neurological examination to localize the dominant compression and plan the surgical sequence. Therefore, I order these tests and we reconvene after results. If MRI shows cord T2 hyperintensity or severe stenosis at both thoracic and cervical levels, we will proceed with thoracic-first decompression (T6-10) because lower extremity weakness and bowel symptoms point to thoracic cord. If MRI shows no T2 signal but clinical progression is ongoing, we will still decompress the most stenotic level responsible for symptoms, likely thoracic, because clinical progression with severe stenosis warrants surgery regardless of T2 signal.
